scenes.visual: Title card 'One Tug, Many Jobs' fades in over three small vignettes in a row: a water strider on a pond, a paper towel corner dipped in a glass with a blue stain creeping up it, and salt grains vanishing into a glass of water. THE WORLD, kept for both films: 16:9, warm cream background, flat cartoon shapes, no molecular structures. Each water molecule is a wide V-shaped block: a large body block for oxygen at the point and two small tip blocks for the hydrogens. COLOUR MAP, same in every scene, in both films and in the lesson's figures: OXYGEN END = RED, labelled 'slightly negative' (δ−); HYDROGEN ENDS = BLUE, labelled 'slightly positive' (δ+); COVALENT BOND inside a molecule = short solid GREY bar; HYDROGEN BOND between molecules = dashed GOLD line; liquid WATER as a substance = pale BLUE fill; SAND = TAN; ENERGY = small ORANGE dots; OIL = pale GREEN droplet; CELLULOSE fibre = light BROWN strand. Anything not computed is labelled 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: Could one fact about one tiny molecule explain three puzzles? An insect stands on a pond, a paper towel drinks water upward, and salt vanishes into a glass.
scenes.visual: The three vignettes play in turn: the strider's feet dimple the surface; the blue stain climbs the towel; salt grains shrink and disappear. A question mark grows above all three, then the camera dives toward the water in the glass.
scenes.narration: Could one fact about one tiny molecule explain three puzzles? An insect stands on a pond, a paper towel drinks water upward, and salt vanishes into a glass.

scenes.tts: Start with one water molecule: one oxygen atom and two hydrogen atoms. Each hydrogen shares electrons with the oxygen in a covalent bond. The molecule is bent, like a wide letter V.
scenes.visual: One V-shaped molecule assembles: a large neutral body block slides in, two small tip blocks attach with short solid GREY bars labelled 'covalent bond: shared electrons'. The molecule tilts to show the bend, with a faint V traced over it.
scenes.narration: Start with one water molecule: one oxygen atom and two hydrogen atoms. Each hydrogen shares electrons with the oxygen in a covalent bond. The molecule is bent, like a wide letter V.

scenes.tts: Oxygen pulls the shared electrons closer. So the oxygen end becomes slightly negative, shown in red. Each hydrogen end becomes slightly positive, shown in blue. A molecule with charged ends is polar.
scenes.caption: Oxygen pulls the shared electrons closer. So the oxygen end becomes slightly negative (δ−), shown in red. Each hydrogen end becomes slightly positive (δ+), shown in blue. A molecule with charged ends is polar.
scenes.visual: A soft grey cloud over the molecule slides toward the body block. The body block turns RED with a 'δ−' tag; the tips turn BLUE with 'δ+' tags. The word 'polar' appears beside it. A small sign below reads 'net charge: 0'.
scenes.narration: Oxygen pulls the shared electrons closer. So the oxygen end becomes slightly negative (δ−), shown in red. Each hydrogen end becomes slightly positive (δ+), shown in blue. A molecule with charged ends is polar.

scenes.tts: Bring in a neighbor. Opposite charges attract, so the blue end of one molecule is drawn to the red end of the next. That weak pull between molecules is a hydrogen bond, drawn as a dashed gold line.
scenes.visual: A second V molecule drifts in and rotates until one of its BLUE tips points at the first molecule's RED body. A dashed GOLD line snaps on between them, labelled 'hydrogen bond: between molecules'. The GREY bars inside each molecule stay drawn solid for contrast.
scenes.narration: Bring in a neighbor. Opposite charges attract, so the blue end of one molecule is drawn to the red end of the next. That weak pull between molecules is a hydrogen bond, drawn as a dashed gold line.

scenes.tts: Liquid water holds countless jostling molecules. Gold lines snap on, break, and form again with new partners. The grey bonds inside each molecule stay put, because they are much stronger.
scenes.visual: Zoom out to a crowd of about thirty V molecules jittering. Dashed GOLD lines flicker on and off between neighbors, re-pairing every second. The GREY bars inside each molecule never flicker. A small label: 'gold lines break and re-form; grey bars stay'.
scenes.narration: Liquid water holds countless jostling molecules. Gold lines snap on, break, and form again with new partners. The grey bonds inside each molecule stay put, because they are much stronger.

scenes.tts: Here is the one idea. Water's charged ends tug on its neighbors, on ions, and on other polar molecules. Now watch it do three jobs.
scenes.visual: A large GOLD 'tug' arrow sweeps over the crowd. The sentence 'Water's charged ends tug on neighbors, ions and polar molecules' types on at the top. Three empty panels slide in below, labelled 1, 2, 3.
scenes.narration: Here is the one idea. Water's charged ends tug on its neighbors, on ions, and on other polar molecules. Now watch it do three jobs.

scenes.tts: Job one is dissolving. Salt is made of charged particles called ions, positive sodium and negative chloride. Water's red ends face each sodium, and its blue ends face each chloride. That pull of opposite charges lifts each ion off the crystal. So water is a solvent.
scenes.visual: Panel 1: a small checkerboard crystal of purple '+ sodium' and green '− chloride' squares sits in pale BLUE water. V molecules turn their RED ends toward a sodium square and their BLUE tips toward a chloride square, then tug; ions peel off one by one, each wrapped in a ring of molecules. The water-to-ion pulls are drawn as thin plain arrows, NOT dashed GOLD lines, with a small on-screen tag 'pull of opposite charges (not a hydrogen bond)'. Label 'solvent'.
scenes.narration: Job one is dissolving. Salt is made of charged particles called ions, positive sodium and negative chloride. Water's red ends face each sodium, and its blue ends face each chloride. That pull of opposite charges lifts each ion off the crystal. So water is a solvent.

scenes.tts: Now add some oil. Oil molecules are mostly nonpolar, with few charged spots to grab. Water molecules tug on each other more than on oil, so the oil stays in its own drop.
scenes.visual: A pale GREEN oil droplet with the label 'mostly nonpolar' drops into panel 1. Water molecules around it turn away and link to each other with GOLD lines; the droplet stays round and separate, then floats up out of the crowd.
scenes.narration: Now add some oil. Oil molecules are mostly nonpolar, with few charged spots to grab. Water molecules tug on each other more than on oil, so the oil stays in its own drop.

scenes.tts: Job two is sticking to itself, called cohesion. At the surface, neighbors pull each molecule sideways and down. So the surface resists being stretched. That is surface tension, and it is still liquid water, not a skin.
scenes.visual: Panel 2: a side view of water. The top row of molecules gets small arrows pointing sideways and down, none pointing up. A strider's leg presses in and the surface dimples like a trampoline but does not break. Labels 'cohesion' then 'surface tension'; a crossed-out word 'skin'.
scenes.narration: Job two is sticking to itself, called cohesion. At the surface, neighbors pull each molecule sideways and down. So the surface resists being stretched. That is surface tension, and it is still liquid water, not a skin.

scenes.tts: Job three is sticking to other things. Paper is made of cellulose fibers, with many polar parts. Water clings to them, and that is adhesion. Each climbing molecule pulls its neighbors up by cohesion. Together they give capillary action.
scenes.visual: Panel 3: a light BROWN cellulose strand stands upright in water, dotted with small red and blue patches marking polar parts. Water molecules latch onto the patches with GOLD lines (label 'adhesion') and drag neighbours up with GOLD lines between molecules (label 'cohesion'). The blue fill creeps up the strand; label 'capillary action'.
scenes.narration: Job three is sticking to other things. Paper is made of cellulose fibers, with many polar parts. Water clings to them, and that is adhesion. Each climbing molecule pulls its neighbors up by cohesion. Together they give capillary action.

scenes.tts: Back to the strider. Its legs are covered in tiny water-repellent hairs. Will water climb those hairs like it climbs the towel? Pause and decide.
scenes.visual: Split screen: on the left the BROWN cellulose strand with water climbing; on the right a strider leg, magnified, covered in fine grey hairs labelled 'water-repellent hairs'. A question mark sits between them.
scenes.narration: Back to the strider. Its legs are covered in tiny water-repellent hairs. Will water climb those hairs like it climbs the towel? Pause and decide.

scenes.visual: Hold the split screen. A small 5-second countdown ring empties in the corner.

scenes.tts: No. Water clings only weakly to water-repellent hairs, so it pulls itself into beads. Surface tension, plus those hairs, lets a small strider stand.
scenes.visual: Water molecules near the hairs find no red or blue patches and pull back into a round bead. The leg rests on the dimpled surface. Labels: 'weak adhesion: water beads up' and 'surface tension + water-repellent hairs'.
scenes.narration: No. Water clings only weakly to water-repellent hairs, so it pulls itself into beads. Surface tension, plus those hairs, lets a small strider stand.

scenes.tts: So one molecule's bent shape and charged ends help explain all three jobs. The same tug helps make water slow to warm, as film two shows.
scenes.visual: The three panels shrink side by side under the GOLD tug arrow: ions pulled apart, a dimpled surface, water climbing a fibre. A fourth small panel fades in at the end showing a thermometer beside a glass of water, labelled 'next: warming'.
scenes.narration: So one molecule's bent shape and charged ends help explain all three jobs. The same tug helps make water slow to warm, as film two shows.

scenes.visual: Hex end card. Line on screen: 'Water's charged ends tug on neighbors, ions and polar molecules.'
